text: ServiceNow is almost always the system of action, not the system of record. The data it needs to act on usually lives somewhere else entirely.

Employee data lives in Workday or SuccessFactors. Infrastructure state lives in monitoring tools. Customer data lives in Salesforce. And after a merger, there's often a whole second ticketing system still holding active tickets. ServiceNow can't act on data it can't see.

Without integration, someone has to notice a new hire in Workday and manually re-type it into ServiceNow before onboarding can even start — hours or days of delay, and a typo waiting to happen. With integration, Workday pushes that data in the moment it's finalized, and onboarding starts automatically, already holding the correct manager, department, and start date.

Integration isn't one-directional. A monitoring tool can push a trigger into ServiceNow, automatically creating an Incident the second it detects an outage, rather than waiting for a human to notice and log a ticket. Just as often, ServiceNow is the one initiating: an approved Change Request calls out to a deployment tool to actually carry out the work, instead of a human reading the approval and clicking through a separate console by hand.

Which direction a given integration needs is dictated by where the triggering event actually happens — not by whichever direction is more convenient to build. A real integration developer has to be comfortable building either one.

Courses one through six built fluency inside ServiceNow itself. This course turns outward — building the pipes that bring in the data ServiceNow doesn't own, and push ServiceNow's own actions out to the systems that need them.
System of action, not system of record — that's the whole reason integration exists. Next up: the three pattern categories that cover almost every integration you'll ever build.
